q: Cells divide on a regular basic to bring about growth and asexual reproduction.
e: True. Cells divide on a regular basic to bring about growth and asexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction copies one parent, often through mitosis.

q: Cells divide on a regular basic to bring about growth and sexual reproduction.
e: False. Ordinary cell division supports growth and asexual reproduction. Sexual reproduction needs meiosis and gametes.

q: Interphase is a period of non-division, which is subdivided into $G_1$, S and $G_2$ stages.
e: True. Interphase is a period of non-division, which is subdivided into G1, S and G2 stages. S is the synthesis stage of interphase when DNA is copied. Interphase is G1, S, and G2, when the cell grows and copies DNA.

q: Interphase is a period of active division, which is subdivided into $G_1$, S and $G_2$ stages.
e: False. Interphase is a non-division growth period. Nuclear division happens in mitosis, not in interphase.

q: In $G_1$ stage, the growth of cell takes place.
e: True. In G1 stage, the growth of cell takes place.

q: In $G_1$ stage, DNA replication is carried out.
e: False. G1 is for cell growth. DNA is copied in S phase, not in G1.

q: DNA replication is carried out in S stage.
e: True. DNA replication is carried out in S stage. DNA replication happens in S phase. DNA is replicated in S phase of interphase.

q: After replication is completed, each chromosome consists of four identical DNA molecules called chromatids.
e: False. It is not true that after replication is completed, each chromosome consists of four identical DNA molecules called chromatids. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere. A chromosome is a DNA molecule with proteins, visible when condensed.

q: Chromatids are joined together at a point called the centromere.
e: True. Chromatids are joined together at a point called the centromere. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere. The centromere is where sister chromatids are held and where spindle fibres attach.

q: Chromatids are joined together at a point called the centrosome.
e: False. It is not true that chromatids are joined together at a point called the centrosome. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere.

q: In $G_2$ stage, the organelles are replicated and the cell grows.
e: True. In G2 stage, the organelles are replicated and the cell grows.

q: Mitosis is a period of active nuclear division and cytokinesis is the separation of cytoplasm.
e: True. Mitosis is a period of active nuclear division and cytokinesis is the separation of cytoplasm. Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm to finish making two cells. Cytoplasm is the fluid and structures inside the cell membrane, around the nucleus.

q: Mitosis is a period of active cytoplasmic division and cytokinesis is the separation of the nucleus.
e: False. Mitosis is a period of active cytoplasmic division and cytokinesis is not the separation of the nucleus. Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm to finish making two cells. Mitosis divides the nucleus so two daughter nuclei get identical chromosomes.

q: Cell division is a strictly regulated process that mostly works without errors.
e: True. Cell division is a strictly regulated process that mostly works without errors.

q: When errors do occur in cell division, they can be catastrophic and cause the development of cancer.
e: True. When errors do occur in cell division, they can be catastrophic and cause the development of cancer. Cancer is uncontrolled cell division after control checkpoints fail.

q: The interphase, the initial stage of the cell cycle, used to be called the resting phase.
e: True. The interphase, the initial stage of the cell cycle, used to be called the resting phase. The cell cycle is growth plus nuclear and cytoplasmic division. The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of growth, DNA copy, and division.

q: During interphase, the normal metabolic processes of the cell stop and no new DNA is produced.
e: False. It is not true that during interphase, the normal metabolic processes of the cell stop and no new DNA is produced. Interphase is G1, S, and G2, when the cell grows and copies DNA. DNA carries the genetic code in a double helix of nucleotides.

q: During mitosis, the chromosomes that are duplicated during interphase are divided to produce two identical daughter cells.
e: True. During mitosis, the chromosomes that are duplicated during interphase are divided to produce two identical daughter cells. Mitosis plus cytokinesis yields two genetically identical daughter cells. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells.

q: Mitosis is divided into four phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
e: True. Mitosis is divided into four phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. In metaphase chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate. In telophase nuclei reform around the two chromosome sets.

q: During prophase, the chromatins become more tightly coiled and condensing into discrete chromosomes.
e: True. During prophase, the chromatins become more tightly coiled and condensing into discrete chromosomes. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells. In prophase chromosomes condense and the spindle starts to form.

q: During prophase, the nuclear envelope forms and the nucleolus appears.
e: False. It is not true that during prophase, the nuclear envelope forms and the nucleolus appears. The nuclear envelope breaks down in prophase and reforms in telophase. The nucleolus vanishes in prophase and returns in telophase.

q: The radial arrays of shorter microtubules around each centriole are called asters.
e: True. The radial arrays of shorter microtubules around each centriole are called asters. Asters are microtubule arrays around the poles in animal mitosis.

q: During metaphase, the chromosomes line up along the metaphase plate (equator) of the cell.
e: True. During metaphase, the chromosomes line up along the metaphase plate (equator) of the cell. The metaphase plate is the equator where chromosomes align. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells.

q: During metaphase, each chromatid becomes attached to the spindle by its telomere.
e: False. It is not true that during metaphase, each chromatid becomes attached to the spindle by its telomere. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere. In metaphase chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate.

q: During anaphase, the chromatids from each pair are pulled, centromere first, towards opposite poles of the cell.
e: True. During anaphase, the chromatids from each pair are pulled, centromere first, towards opposite poles of the cell. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere. The centromere is where sister chromatids are held and where spindle fibres attach.

q: During anaphase, the centromeres do not divide and sister chromatids remain attached.
e: False. It is not true that during anaphase, the centromeres do not divide and sister chromatids remain attached. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere. In anaphase sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.

q: At the end of anaphase, the chromatids are now called chromosomes, as each is an identical copy of chromosome.
e: True. At the end of anaphase, the chromatids are now called chromosomes, as each is an identical copy of chromosome. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere.

q: During telophase, the spindle fibres break down and nuclear envelopes reform around the two sets of chromosomes.
e: True. During telophase, the spindle fibres break down and nuclear envelopes reform around the two sets of chromosomes. Two nuclear envelopes form in telophase. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells.

q: During telophase, the chromosomes begin to coil and becoming more dense.
e: False. It is not true that during telophase, the chromosomes begin to coil and becoming more dense. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells. In telophase nuclei reform around the two chromosome sets.

q: The final phase of the cell cycle is cytokinesis, when the cytoplasm divides.
e: True. The final phase of the cell cycle is cytokinesis, when the cytoplasm divides. The cell cycle is growth plus nuclear and cytoplasmic division. Many metabolic reactions run in the cytoplasm.

q: In animal cells, a cellulose cell wall builds up from the inside of the cell outwards during cytokinesis.
e: False. It is not true that in animal cells, a cellulose cell wall builds up from the inside of the cell outwards during cytokinesis. Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm to finish making two cells. Cellulose is the beta-glucose polymer that makes plant cell walls rigid.

q: In plant cells, a cellulose cell wall builds up from the inside of the cell outwards during cytokinesis.
e: True. In plant cells, a cellulose cell wall builds up from the inside of the cell outwards during cytokinesis. Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm to finish making two cells. Cellulose is the beta-glucose polymer that makes plant cell walls rigid.

q: Meiosis is a type of nuclear division that happens only in sex organs.
e: True. Meiosis is a type of nuclear division that happens only in sex organs. Meiosis is reduction division that makes haploid gametes and shuffles alleles.

q: Meiosis is called reduction division because the cells that are formed have half the number of chromosomes.
e: True. Meiosis is called reduction division because the cells that are formed have half the number of chromosomes. Meiosis I is the reduction division that halves chromosome number. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells.

q: In animals, the somatic cells are formed directly from meiosis.
e: False. It is not true that in animals, the somatic cells are formed directly from meiosis. Meiosis is reduction division that makes haploid gametes and shuffles alleles.

q: The formation of sperm is called spermatogenesis, while that of ovum is called oogenesis.
e: True. The formation of sperm is called spermatogenesis, while that of ovum is called oogenesis. Spermatogenesis is meiosis that produces sperm. Oogenesis is meiosis that produces eggs.

q: In flowering plants, meiosis forms special male cells called microspores and female cells called megaspores.
e: True. In flowering plants, meiosis forms special male cells called microspores and female cells called megaspores. Flowering is the mark of angiosperms. Meiosis is reduction division that makes haploid gametes and shuffles alleles.

q: In meiosis, two nuclear divisions produce four haploid daughter cells, each with its own unique combination of genetic material.
e: True. In meiosis, two nuclear divisions produce four haploid daughter cells, each with its own unique combination of genetic material. Mitosis plus cytokinesis yields two genetically identical daughter cells. Meiosis is reduction division that makes haploid gametes and shuffles alleles.

q: During prophase I of meiosis, homologous pairs of chromosomes pair along their lengths which is called synapsis.
e: True. During prophase I of meiosis, homologous pairs of chromosomes pair along their lengths which is called synapsis. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells. In prophase chromosomes condense and the spindle starts to form.

q: During prophase I of meiosis, crossing over occurs between sister chromatids.
e: False. It is not true that during prophase I of meiosis, crossing over occurs between sister chromatids. Crossing over in prophase I swaps DNA between homologous chromosomes. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere.

q: During metaphase I, homologous pairs of chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate.
e: True. During metaphase I, homologous pairs of chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate. The metaphase plate is the equator where chromosomes align. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells.

q: During anaphase I, the centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate.
e: False. It is not true that during anaphase I, the centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA copies joined at a centromere. In anaphase sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.

q: No chromosome replication occurs between meiosis I and meiosis II.
e: True. No chromosome replication occurs between meiosis I and meiosis II. Meiosis halves the chromosome number for gametes. A chromosome is a DNA molecule with proteins, visible when condensed.

q: In prophase I of meiosis, crossing over introduces genetic variation as the chromatids may break and recombine.
e: True. In prophase I of meiosis, crossing over introduces genetic variation as the chromatids may break and recombine. Meiosis, crossing over, and random fertilisation generate genetic variation. Crossing over in prophase I swaps DNA between homologous chromosomes.

q: The branch of biology known as Genetics deals with the inheritance of characteristics or traits from parents to their progeny.
e: True. The branch of biology known as Genetics deals with the inheritance of characteristics or traits from parents to their progeny. Biology systematically studies plants, animals, and microorganisms.

q: The physical and chemical characteristics that make up the appearance of an organism are known as its genotype.
e: False. It is not true that the physical and chemical characteristics that make up the appearance of an organism are known as its genotype. Genotype is the allele combination an organism carries.

q: The phenotype of an individual is determined by its genotype.
e: True. The phenotype of an individual is determined by its genotype. Phenotype is the observed trait produced by genotype and environment. Genotype is the allele combination an organism carries.

q: The genotype is a total combination of genes and their alleles received from the individuals parents.
e: True. The genotype is a total combination of genes and their alleles received from the individuals parents. Genotype is the allele combination an organism carries. Alleles are different versions of the same gene.

q: The phenotype is solely determined by the genotype and is not affected by the environment.
e: False. It is not true that the phenotype is solely determined by the genotype and is not affected by the environment. The environment is everything around an organism, biotic and abiotic. Phenotype is the observed trait produced by genotype and environment.

q: Genes are unit of hereditary characteristics and are a length of DNA that is the code for making a protein molecule.
e: True. Genes are unit of hereditary characteristics and are a length of DNA that is the code for making a protein molecule. Proteins are polymers of amino acids with many structural and catalytic jobs. DNA carries the genetic code in a double helix of nucleotides.

q: The different forms of each gene are known as alleles.
e: True. The different forms of each gene are known as alleles. Alleles are different versions of the same gene. A gene is a DNA stretch that codes for a product, usually a protein.

q: When the two alleles are different, the individual is homozygous to this gene.
e: False. It is not true that when the two alleles are different, the individual is homozygous to this gene. Homozygous means both alleles of a gene are the same. Alleles are different versions of the same gene.

q: When the two alleles are the same and dominant, the individual is homozygous dominant.
e: True. When the two alleles are the same and dominant, the individual is homozygous dominant. Homozygous means both alleles of a gene are the same. A dominant allele shows in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.

q: Mendel's first law is also known as the Law of segregation.
e: True. Mendel's first law is also known as the Law of segregation. Segregation is the splitting of allele pairs when gametes form.

q: The law of segregation states that during the formation of gametes, the two traits carried by each parent separate.
e: True. The law of segregation states that during the formation of gametes, the two traits carried by each parent separate. Segregation is the splitting of allele pairs when gametes form. Gametes are sex cells: sperm and eggs, produced by meiosis.

q: A monohybrid cross is a mating in which two different genes are analyzed in the cross.
e: False. A monohybrid cross is not a mating in which two different genes are analyzed in the cross. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: Mendel's second law is also known as the Law of independent assortment.
e: True. Mendel's second law is also known as the Law of independent assortment. Independent assortment is the random sorting of different chromosome pairs into gametes.

q: The law of independent assortment states that during gamete formation, the genes for one trait are not inherited along with the genes for another trait.
e: True. The law of independent assortment states that during gamete formation, the genes for one trait are not inherited along with the genes for another trait. Independent assortment is the random sorting of different chromosome pairs into gametes.

q: A dihybrid cross is used to show the inheritance of two different characteristics, controlled by two genes.
e: True. A dihybrid cross is used to show the inheritance of two different characteristics, controlled by two genes. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: Testcross is used to determine the genotype of an individual exhibiting a recessive phenotype.
e: False. It is not true that testcross is used to determine the genotype of an individual exhibiting a recessive phenotype. Phenotype is the observed trait produced by genotype and environment. A recessive allele shows only when two copies are present.

q: The testcross parent is always homozygous recessive for all of the genes under consideration.
e: True. The testcross parent is always homozygous recessive for all of the genes under consideration. Homozygous means both alleles of a gene are the same. A recessive allele shows only when two copies are present.

q: A homozygous dominant individual will produce two kinds of gametes with equal frequency.
e: False. It is not true that a homozygous dominant individual will produce two kinds of gametes with equal frequency. Homozygous means both alleles of a gene are the same. A dominant allele shows in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.

q: Backcross is done in order to achieve offspring with a genotype closer to that of the parents.
e: True. Backcross is done in order to achieve offspring with a genotype closer to that of the parents. Genotype is the allele combination an organism carries.

q: In the backcross, the $F_1$ progeny are mated back to one of their parents.
e: True. In the backcross, the F1 progeny are mated back to one of their parents.

q: The testcross is different in that a homozygous dominant is always used as the testcross parent.
e: False. The testcross is different in that a homozygous dominant is does not always used as the testcross parent. Homozygous means both alleles of a gene are the same. A dominant allele shows in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.

q: Alleles that lack complete dominant and recessive relationships and are both observed phenotypically are called codominant.
e: True. Alleles that lack complete dominant and recessive relationships and are both observed phenotypically are called codominant. Codominant alleles both show fully in the heterozygote, as in AB blood. A recessive allele shows only when two copies are present.

q: In codominance, the heterozygous genotype gives rise to a phenotype that is a blending of both alleles.
e: False. In codominance, the heterozygous genotype gives rise to a phenotype that is not a blending of both alleles. Heterozygous means the two alleles of a gene are different. Phenotype is the observed trait produced by genotype and environment.

q: For codominant alleles, all uppercase base symbols with different superscripts are used.
e: True. For codominant alleles, all uppercase base symbols with different superscripts are used. Codominant alleles both show fully in the heterozygote, as in AB blood. Alleles are different versions of the same gene.

q: Red and white coat colours of the Shorthorn breed of cattle represent a classical example of codominant allele.
e: True. Red and white coat colours of the Shorthorn breed of cattle represent a classical example of codominant allele. Codominant alleles both show fully in the heterozygote, as in AB blood. Alleles are different versions of the same gene.

q: If a dominant allele of a gene does not completely mask the effects of its recessive allele, it is called incomplete dominance.
e: True. If a dominant allele of a gene does not completely mask the effects of its recessive allele, it is called incomplete dominance. Incomplete dominance blends the heterozygote, as in pink from red and white. A recessive allele shows only when two copies are present.

q: When there are more than two alleles of a gene, it is referred to as multiple alleles.
e: True. When there are more than two alleles of a gene, it is referred to as multiple alleles. Multiple alleles means a gene has more than two possible versions in the population, as in ABO blood groups. Alleles are different versions of the same gene.

q: In the ABO blood group system, the allele $I^A$ for the A antigen is recessive to the allele $I^B$ for the B antigen.
e: False. It is not true that in the ABO blood group system, the allele I^A for the A antigen is recessive to the allele I^B for the B antigen. ABO blood groups come from multiple alleles of one gene. A recessive allele shows only when two copies are present.

q: Both $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant and both are completely dominant to the allele $i$, which fails to specify any detectable antigenic structure.
e: True. Both I^A and I^B are codominant and both are completely dominant to the allele i, which fails to specify any detectable antigenic structure. Codominant alleles both show fully in the heterozygote, as in AB blood. A dominant allele shows in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.

q: The blood group AB is referred to as the universal donor.
e: False. It is not true that the blood group AB is referred to as the universal donor. ABO blood groups come from multiple alleles of one gene. O is the universal donor for red cells because it lacks A and B antigens.

q: The blood group O can transfuse to any of all four groups, as it has neither A antigen nor B antigen.
e: True. The blood group O can transfuse to any of all four groups, as it has neither A antigen nor B antigen. ABO blood groups come from multiple alleles of one gene. An antigen is a molecule the immune system can recognise.

q: In man, and apparently in all other mammals, the presence of the Y chromosome may determine a tendency to maleness.
e: True. In man, and apparently in all other mammals, the presence of the Y chromosome may determine a tendency to maleness. A chromosome is a DNA molecule with proteins, visible when condensed. The Y chromosome carries factors for maleness.

q: Normal males are chromosomally XX and females are XY.
e: False. It is not true that normal males are chromosomally XX and females are XY.

q: Since the male produces two kinds of gametes as far as the sex chromosomes are concerned, he is said to be the heterogametic sex.
e: True. Since the male produces two kinds of gametes as far as the sex chromosomes are concerned, he is said to be the heterogametic sex. Human males are heterogametic because they make X and Y sperm. Chromosomes carry genes; humans have 46 in diploid cells.

q: A mutation is a change in a gene or a chromosome that may cause a change in a phenotypic characteristic.
e: True. A mutation is a change in a gene or a chromosome that may cause a change in a phenotypic characteristic. A chromosome is a DNA molecule with proteins, visible when condensed. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait.

q: Mutations that occur in body cells will be passed on to the next generation.
e: False. It is not true that mutations that occur in body cells will be passed on to the next generation.

q: Only mutation in sex cells (gametes), or in the cell that divide to form gametes, can be passed on to the next generation.
e: True. Only mutation in sex cells (gametes), or in the cell that divide to form gametes, can be passed on to the next generation. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait. Gametes are sex cells: sperm and eggs, produced by meiosis.

q: Chromosome mutations usually result in the death of the cells formed.
e: True. Chromosome mutations usually result in the death of the cells formed. Chromosome mutations change structure or number of whole chromosomes. A chromosome is a DNA molecule with proteins, visible when condensed.

q: Trisomy of chromosome 21 is a relatively common chromosome mutation that results in Down's syndrome.
e: True. Trisomy of chromosome 21 is a relatively common chromosome mutation that results in Down's syndrome. Down's syndrome comes from an extra chromosome 21. A chromosome is a DNA molecule with proteins, visible when condensed.

q: Down's syndrome is more common in babies born by women under 20 years of age.
e: False. It is not true that down's syndrome is more common in babies born by women under 20 years of age. Down's syndrome comes from an extra chromosome 21. An extra chromosome 21 produces Down's syndrome.

q: A change in the nucleotide sequences of a DNA molecule is termed as gene mutation.
e: True. A change in the nucleotide sequences of a DNA molecule is termed as gene mutation. A gene mutation changes the base sequence of one gene. A nucleotide is a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogen base.

q: Albinism is caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for the enzyme that produce melanin.
e: True. Albinism is caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for the enzyme that produce melanin. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed reactions without being used up.

q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for CFTR protein that transport chloride ions.
e: True. Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for CFTR protein that transport chloride ions. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait. Proteins are polymers of amino acids with many structural and catalytic jobs.

q: Sickle-cell anemia is caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for the $\alpha$-chain of haemoglobin.
e: False. It is not true that sickle-cell anemia is caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for the alpha-chain of haemoglobin. Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen for transport. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait.

q: Huntington's disease is caused by a mutation in HD gene located on chromosome 4.
e: True. Huntington's disease is caused by a mutation in HD gene located on chromosome 4. A chromosome is a DNA molecule with proteins, visible when condensed. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait.

q: Mutations occur naturally at random, but the rate at which they occur is increased by exposure to radiation and some chemicals.
e: True. Mutations occur naturally at random, but the rate at which they occur is increased by exposure to radiation and some chemicals.

q: Ultra-violet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays are the most damaging mutagens.
e: True. Ultra-violet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays are the most damaging mutagens. Physical mutagens include radiation; chemical mutagens include some drugs and pollutants.

q: Benzpyrene in cigarette smoke causes mutation.
e: True. Benzpyrene in cigarette smoke causes mutation. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait.

q: The agents that cause mutation are called mutagens.
e: True. The agents that cause mutation are called mutagens. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait. Physical mutagens include radiation; chemical mutagens include some drugs and pollutants.

q: Variation is the differences that exist within a species.
e: True. Variation is the differences that exist within a species. A species is a group of organisms that can breed to produce fertile offspring.

q: Gene mutation is the only way in which completely new genetic material is produced.
e: True. Gene mutation is the only way in which completely new genetic material is produced. A gene mutation changes the base sequence of one gene. A mutation is a change in DNA that may change a trait.

q: Continuous variation has a clear cut distinction between the different traits of a characteristic.
e: False. It is not true that continuous variation has a clear cut distinction between the different traits of a characteristic. Continuous culture keeps adding nutrients and taking product for a long run.

q: Continuous variation is caused by polygenic effects found in a population.
e: True. Continuous variation is caused by polygenic effects found in a population. A population is all the individuals of one species in an area. Continuous culture keeps adding nutrients and taking product for a long run.

q: Height, weight, intelligence, and skin colour are examples of continuous variation.
e: True. Height, weight, intelligence, and skin colour are examples of continuous variation. Continuous culture keeps adding nutrients and taking product for a long run. Skin is a surface for some heat exchange and a barrier, but most large animals also need lungs or gills.

q: Discontinuous variation has a clear cut distinction between two traits.
e: True. Discontinuous variation has a clear cut distinction between two traits. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: Ability or inability to roll the tongue is an example of continuous variation.
e: False. Ability or inability to roll the tongue is not an example of continuous variation. Continuous culture keeps adding nutrients and taking product for a long run.

q: Discontinuous variations are carried by single gene with different alleles.
e: True. Discontinuous variations are carried by single gene with different alleles. Alleles are different versions of the same gene. A gene is a DNA stretch that codes for a product, usually a protein.

q: Nature refers to all of the genes and hereditary factors that influence physical characteristics of an organism.
e: True. Nature refers to all of the genes and hereditary factors that influence physical characteristics of an organism.

q: Nurture refers to all the genetic variables that impact on the character.
e: False. It is not true that nurture refers to all the genetic variables that impact on the character.

q: The basic characteristics of every individual are the result of the genes they have inherited from their parents.
e: True. The basic characteristics of every individual are the result of the genes they have inherited from their parents.

q: An apple tree seed will never grow into an oak tree, which is an example of nurture.
e: False. An apple tree seed will never grow into an oak tree, which is not an example of nurture. Seed plants are gymnosperms and angiosperms.

q: A scar as a result of an accident is an example of environmental variation, not genetic.
e: True. A scar as a result of an accident is an example of environmental variation, not genetic.

q: Genetically identical plants grown under different conditions of light will look identical.
e: False. It is not true that genetically identical plants grown under different conditions of light will look identical. Mitosis makes genetically identical body cells for growth and repair.

q: Features such as eye colour, nose shape, gender, and dimples are the results of genetic information inherited from parents.
e: True. Features such as eye colour, nose shape, gender, and dimples are the results of genetic information inherited from parents.
